## Time


### `clock`

```
clock : Chan Int
```


### `ticks`

```
ticks : Sig Int
```

The sample index — 0, 1, 2, … — one instant per sample.  A synth reads
its own position in time off this rather than counting.


### `seconds`

```
seconds t : Float -> Int
```

Seconds as a number of samples.


### `elapsed`

```
elapsed : Sig Float
```

**How long the program has been running, in seconds.**  The clock a
piece with no score has.

`beat` is the other one and is a *score's* — it needs a `bpm`, so an
unscored synth naming it is told there is no tempo to answer with.  A
drone, a soundscape or anything else that varies over its own duration
rather than over a bar wants this instead, and `on <points> elapsed` is
what reading an envelope against it looks like.


## Signals are numbers


### `Num (Sig Float)`  <sub>instance</sub>

```
instance Num (Sig Float) where
```


**The one that changes how a synth reads.**  `spec/frp_lesson.md` puts
Fran beside this language and the difference is not the combinators, it
is that in Fran a behaviour is a value: `stretch (abs wiggle) charlotte`
applies ordinary functions to something that varies, and nowhere says so.
Here the same thought had to be spelled `zipSig (x y => x * y) tone env`
— the plumbing named at every join, in code whose subject is the sound.

It need not be.  `+`, `-` and `*` are `Num`'s methods, an instance is
ordinary code, and `addSig`/`subSig`/`mulSig` were already written next
door: `tone * env` is a definition away, and it is *the same graph* — the
instance is where the `zipSig` went, not an interpretation layer.

What it cost was one gap in the compiler rather than any new machinery:
a generated method supercombinator carried no type, so the audio fragment
— which asks every definition its type — could not judge one and refused
them all by the name of their instance head.  `elaborate._method_type`
is that gap, closed.


### `Floating (Sig Float)`  <sub>instance</sub>

```
instance Floating (Sig Float) where
```

And the same for a literal with a point in it, which is the one a synth
actually writes: `0.5 + wiggle * 0.25` is the shape it looks like.


## Parameters


### `mkKnob`

```
mkKnob v : a -> Sig a
```

A parameter, and what it holds before anything arrives.

**Polymorphic, and it took a change to the fragment to be.**  A signal
definition is *inlined* at every use, at that use's own type, so a
`mkKnob 0.6` is a `Float` channel and a `mkKnob 40` an `Int` one and no
`a` survives into the graph.  The checker used to judge a definition by
its declared type rather than by what becomes of it, and refused this —
`fixme.md` F96's mistake in a second place — so there were two names,
`mkKnob` and `mkKnobInt`, for one idea.

The type decides the slider an environment draws: a `Float` runs
0.0 .. 1.0, because every `Float` a synth takes a knob for is already a
fraction, and an `Int` runs 0 .. 100.


### `Wrap`  <sub>class</sub>

```
class Wrap a where
```

**Fractional part.**  Keeps an accumulating phase inside 0.0 .. 1.0.

A class because the convention says a plain verb is *a transformation,
at whatever type*, and this one had been a transformation at exactly one
— so `wrap` over a signal meant writing the `map` out.  `synth.ges` adds
the two stereo instances, where `Stereo` is declared.


### `tau`

```
tau : Float
```

Turns, not radians.  One place for 2π, and the same 0..1 phase every
other oscillator here takes — so `sineOf` substitutes for `sawOf` in any
chain rather than needing its own convention.


### `sineOf`

```
sineOf p : Float -> Float
```

A sine, from the same phase.  The one oscillator that is not arithmetic
on a ramp, and the reason `spec/liveaudio.md`'s open question 2 had to
be answered before it could exist.


### `Gate`  <sub>data</sub>

```
Gate := Gate Int Int
```

**When** a note began and when it was released — half of what a
`voices` bank hands a voice, the other half being the program's own
payload.

The two arrive as *two signals*: `voice : Sig Gate -> Sig Key -> Sig
Float`.  They used to arrive as one, `Sig (Played Key)` with
`Played a := Played Int Int a`, and every voice began by taking that
record apart to get at whichever half it wanted — an envelope wants the
timing and a pitch wants the payload, and almost nothing wants both.
The bank had them apart already: `gateAt` and `offAt` are channels of
their own, and the bundling was work it did on the way out.  So the
split removes a record, two zips per voice and a projection from every
instrument (`spec/frp_lesson.md`).

Both are **1-based** sample indices, and zero means *nothing*: `on = 0`
is a voice that has never played, `off = 0` one that is still held.  That
is what makes an untouched bank silent from its channels' own defaults,
with nothing a host must remember to send.


### `FromMIDI`  <sub>class</sub>

```
class FromMIDI a where
```

How a MIDI note becomes a bank's payload — and whether it does at all.

`Nothing` **declines** the note, which is what makes this one method
rather than a routing table beside it: a bank that only wants channel 2,
or only the notes below middle C, says so here in ordinary code.

It says the payload *can* come from MIDI, not that a given bank listens.
Two banks may carry the same payload — `duet.ges`'s `lead` and `bass`
both carry `Pitched` — so they share this instance and nothing in the
type could tell them apart.  Which of them listens is the environment's
switch, not the program's.
`noteOn channel pitch velocity`.


### `Notable`  <sub>class</sub>

```
class Notable a where
```

What a reader needs from a note — `FromMIDI`'s other road, half of
the way back: not the MIDI note again, just where it sits and how
hard it was struck.  The score box reads payloads through this
(`spec/scorebox.md`), because the alternative is trusting that a
record's fields happen to sit in `(key, velocity)` order, which is
a convention the type checker never sees and `Tone (toFloat v /
127.0) n` breaks silently.

Not `pitchOf`/`velOf`, which pieces already define as their own
helpers — a class must not collide with the names its authors were
taught to write.


### `Notable Int`  <sub>instance</sub>

```
instance Notable Int where
```

The bare note: a `[: Int :]` melody carries its key number
directly, and the velocity is the 64 that `prog` itself assigns —
so the box agrees with the renderer about how hard an unmarked
note is played.


### `Plain`

```
Plain : Int
```

**How a note is played, as against which note it is** — `spec/annotations.md`.

A manner is a *hint the voice interprets*, not a quantity the score
chose.  On a violin staccato is a bow stroke whose shortness is a
consequence, and accent is bow speed rather than a velocity number; a
pad has no bow.  So a mark that meant `duration * 0.5` would be wrong
for both.  The score says how it should be played and each voice says
what it can do — the same split `Notable` above is the other half of.

**A set in one `Int`, and both halves of that are forced.**  One
number because every payload field becomes a control channel and a
control value is one slot — a list or an enum field is refused by the
bank expander, which is the whole reason this is bits and not a
datatype.  A *set* because a note may be accented and staccato at
once, which any violinist writes on one head, and an ordinal would
have made them exclusive by accident.

### `asks`

```
asks ms m : Int -> Int -> Bool
```

Does this note ask for that manner?  **The one place the encoding is
read**, so no voice ever writes arithmetic about bits, and the day the
set outgrows an `Int` only this line changes.


### `Mannered`  <sub>class</sub>

```
class Mannered a where
```

What a voice needs from a note to play it the way it is written.

Separate from `Notable` rather than folded into it, because they
answer to different readers: the score box reads `Notable` to *draw* a
note, and a voice reads this to *play* one.  A piece may want either
without the other, and `manner _ = Plain` below is why asking costs a
melody nothing.


### `Mannered Int`  <sub>instance</sub>

```
instance Mannered Int where
```

The bare note: a `[: Int :]` melody is a key number and nothing else,
so it asks for nothing — the same promise `instance Notable Int` makes
about velocity.  **An unmarked note is not a special case**, it is a
note whose set is empty, and every `asks` on it answers `False`
without a branch anywhere else.


### `lowpass`

```
lowpass k s : Sig Float -> Sig Float -> Sig Float
```

A one-pole lowpass, as a *signal transformation*.  A coefficient near 0
is very smooth, near 1 lets everything through.  This is the shape the whole
design is for: a signal in, a signal out, state held by `scan`.

The coefficient is a signal, and a number is one — `lowpass 0.1 s` is
the fixed filter it always was, and a coefficient an envelope moves is
the same function.  A `Float`-typed expression needs the lift: `lowpass
(!k) s`.


### `Clip`  <sub>class</sub>

```
class Clip a where
```

**Keep a sample in range** — hard-limit it to -1.0 .. 1.0, which is
what a renderer can write and anything beyond is what a renderer
clips for you, badly.

A class for the reason `wrap` is one, and `synth.ges` adds the stereo
instances beside it.  `softClip` is the version that curves into the
limit instead of cornering at it.

### The beat clock under a tempo envelope


#### `LowpassIn`  <sub>data</sub>

```
LowpassIn := LowpassIn Float Float
```

`lowpass`'s sample and coefficient arriving together — a zip needs a
carrier and a tuple has no layout in the fragment.


#### `lowpassNext`

```
lowpassNext y p : Float -> LowpassIn -> Float
```

`lowpass`, one sample: the state chases `x` by `c` of the distance.


#### `beatOpen`

```
beatOpen b0 y0 rest t : Float -> Float -> List Envelope -> Float -> Float
```

Before the first point the tempo is the first tempo, held — so the beat
clock is linear there, and the first point falls at `60·b₀/y₀`.


#### `beatWalk`

```
beatWalk t0 b0 y0 rest t : Float -> Float -> Float -> List Envelope -> Float -> Float
```

One segment at a time, carrying where it starts in *both* coordinates.
`dt` is the trapezoid — a linear ramp covers its beats in the time its
mean tempo would — and `k` is the slope in bpm per second.


#### `beatSeg`

```

```



#### `beatK`

